subject: Accounting for area in poisson models

messages.author: 863a0481c01d0ecd
messages.subject: Accounting for area in poisson models
parts:
It looks like my previous message didn't go through.

I am implementing a Poisson model of the number of occurrences in different district units. I would like to find the best way to account for differences in area of the units in the model.

Following similar examples such as the oral and larynx cancer examples from Martino and Rue (2010) and the suicide and low birth weight ones from Blangiardo e t al 2013, I cannot find any way the area of the administrative units was taken into account. Could anyone explain me why? is this something that is somehow implicitly incorporated in the models?

Thanks for any help,

Victor.

messages.author: bbb9357156c132fe
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Accounting for area in poisson models
parts:
Hi Victor,
That is in the E parameter in the inla call, which denotes the baseline risk. The linear predictor eta is then modelling the log relative risk.

In formulas:

y_i ~ Poisson( E_i*exp(eta_i) )
eta_i = 1 + cov_i + u_i   (here u is a spatial effect)

is implemented as 

r = inla(y ~ 1 +cov + f(u, model="bym"), family= "poisson", data = data.frame(y, cov, u), E = E)

Hope this makes sense.

D

messages.author: 863a0481c01d0ecd
messages.subject: Re: Accounting for area in poisson models
parts:
Thank you all for your helpful posts. 

I am trying to predict the number of occurrences in administrative districts using a GAM type model.  Districts are composed by cells of constant size and each cell can adopt a value of 0 or 1 with 1 being considered an occurrence. 

Following your advice, I defined E as the total number of cells in each district (ncells). Now my problem is that my model seems to be overfitting as you can see in the attached cov1.pdf. Could anyone give me a clue about why this is happening?

Here is the representation of the model:
y_i ~ Poisson( E_i*exp(eta_i) )

eta_i = 1 + f(cov1) + cov2 + spatial effects

Here is the code for inla:

formula=occurrences~f(inla.group(cov1), model="rw2") + cov2 +  f(district_id, model="bym", graph=g)

cheap.mod= inla(formula, data=Data, family="poisson", verbose=TRUE, control.fixed=list(prec.intercept=0.1, expand.factor.strategy='inla'), control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian", int.strategy="eb"),  E=ncells) 

I grouped cov1 to reduce the number of unique values and tried to change the n option in inla.group() but it does not fix the problem. 

Following a previous publication, I used the formula below to transform the response (occurrences) into normal and then fitted the model as a gaussian process:

newresponse=log(occurrences/ncells)

The results from this transformed model look way better and make sense based on my hypotheses (see attached transfmod_cov1.pdf). However I am not convinced about the implications of such transformation.The model also requires to remove all districts with zero occurrences, which might carry important information.

Any pointers will be highly appreciated.

Best,

Victor.
